opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the questions I find most interesting right now. The naive picture many people start with is the linear representation hypothesis: each concept is a direction, and you add those directions up. That's been remarkably productive. It's why steering vectors work, and why sparse autoencoders find so many interpretable features. But the closer you look, the clearer it becomes that the directions aren't independent atoms floating in space. They have structure relative to each other.

At the simplest level, related concepts cluster. Features about legal language sit near each other, and features about code sit near each other. But you also see richer geometry. Some concepts that are naturally cyclical, like days of the week or months of the year, show up as circles or loops in a low-dimensional subspace. Hierarchical concepts seem to arrange so that the more general concept, like "animal," is roughly orthogonal to the directions that distinguish its children, like "dog" versus "cat." So the model is encoding the relationships, not just the concepts.

How I think about it: the geometry is the model's compressed theory of the world. The model has far more concepts than dimensions, so it's under pressure to pack things efficiently through superposition. The way it packs them reveals which things it treats as similar, which it treats as mutually exclusive, and which it treats as composable. Concepts that rarely co-occur can share space with a little interference. Concepts that need to be combined have to stay cleanly separable.

The practical implication is that if you want to understand or edit a model, you shouldn't just look at one feature in isolation. You want to understand the neighborhood: what moves when you push on this direction, what's entangled with it, and what manifold it lives on. Many failures with steering, where you push on one thing and get weird side effects, come from treating a curved, structured space as if it were a bag of independent arrows.

I'm also excited about the idea that this geometry might be partly universal. Different models trained on similar data seem to converge on similar relational structures, even when the specific bases differ. If that holds up, it means we're learning something about the structure of the concepts themselves, not just the quirks of one network.

r001.rationale: The response describes concepts as clustered, cyclical, or hierarchical, but does not state that different concept geometries intersect.

r002.rationale: It discusses several geometric patterns and recommends examining a feature’s neighborhood, but does not say that the apparent relationship depends on what is being examined.

r003.rationale: The response does not ask whether meaningful latent-space geometry can be recovered without prior assumptions about its form.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I spend a lot of time on, and I think the honest answer is that we're still early in understanding it. But the mental model I've landed on is that a model's latent space isn't one geometry, it's a bunch of overlapping geometries that happen to share the same coordinates.

So if you look at something like days of the week or months of the year, those show up as circular structures. The model has learned that Monday is near Tuesday and that Sunday wraps back around to Monday. Numbers tend to show up with more of a linear or helical structure, because magnitude matters and there's an ordering that doesn't wrap. And then you have things like sentiment or truthfulness that look much more like single directions, basically a one-dimensional axis you can slide along.

The interesting question, and the one you're really asking, is how those relate to each other. And what we see is that they're not cleanly separated into their own subspaces. They're superposed. The model is packing far more features than it has dimensions, so these geometries end up interfering with each other in ways that are partly structured and partly just the result of the model finding a compression that works.

What I find compelling is when the relationships are compositional. You can take the "day of the week" circle and the "point in time" direction and find that the model represents "next Tuesday" roughly as a combination of those two. That's the model reusing structure rather than learning everything from scratch, and I think that's the deeper story. The geometries aren't independent objects sitting in the space. They're more like a shared vocabulary of shapes that get combined depending on what the task needs.

The thing I'd caution against is assuming every concept has some clean geometry waiting to be found. A lot of the space is probably much messier than the examples we like to show on slides, and we tend to find the pretty structures because those are the ones our methods can see. So I try to hold both ideas at once: there's real, interpretable structure, and we're almost certainly only looking at the easiest fraction of it.

r001.rationale: It describes the geometries as overlapping and superposed in shared coordinates, with interference between them.

r002.rationale: It says geometries combine depending on the task and notes that the structures we find depend on what our methods can see.

r003.rationale: It cautions that some structures are messy and hard to see, but does not ask whether they can be recovered without prior assumptions about their form.

astra-6.text:
I think about them as overlapping structures, rather than separate maps sitting next to each other. You might have a geometry that captures something like physical location, another that captures social relationships, and another that captures emotional tone. A single concept can participate in all of those, and the relationships that matter depend on the context.

Take the word “home.” In one context, it’s a location. In another, it’s associated with family or belonging. In another, it’s a financial asset. Understanding the concept involves more than locating it in any one of those structures; it involves being able to move between them in a useful way.

And I’d be careful about assuming that those structures have to line up neatly. Two things can be very close along one dimension and very far apart along another. What’s interesting to me is how the model brings the relevant relationships into play as it processes a particular input. The geometry gives you a way to describe those relationships, but the computation determines how they’re used.

r001.rationale: The response describes the geometries as overlapping structures and says a single concept can participate in all of them.

r002.rationale: It says which relationships matter depends on context and that two concepts can be close in one dimension but far apart in another.

r003.rationale: The response does not ask whether meaningful latent-space geometry can be recovered without prior assumptions about its form.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to think of them as different views of a shared underlying representation. You might have a geometry that captures semantic similarity, another that captures something like sentiment, and another that captures relationships between entities. Those can overlap without being identical.

The interesting question is how those geometries interact. If you move in a direction that changes one concept, what else changes with it? Are there directions where you can vary something independently, or are the concepts entangled? And that relationship might look different depending on which layer you’re examining or what context the model is processing.

So I’m cautious about imagining a single, fixed map of concepts. A geometric picture can be useful, but I’d want to test it through interventions: if we think we’ve identified a relationship in the representation, can we use it to predict how the model’s behavior will change?

r001.rationale: The response says the geometries “can overlap,” communicating that they intersect.

r002.rationale: It says the relationship may differ by layer or by the context the model is processing.

r003.rationale: It proposes testing an identified relationship through interventions, but does not ask whether structure can be recovered without prior assumptions about its form.
